title: One tree, one week
hookLine: visit the same tree daily, and let one tree teach you how much changes in a week
carry: something ordinary becomes someone you visit

lines: WHAT STAYS STILL, WE STOP SEEING.
cards: There's probably a tree you pass without seeing it. On the way to the bus, outside the office window, at the corner where the dog always stops. It's easy to know a phone's lock screen better than that tree.
That's not a flaw; it's how attention works. What stays still, people stop looking at. Clouds get the eye because they move.
A tree seems to do nothing at all. So today, not a new tree, not a well-known one. The same one, every day, for a week.

teach.h: A TREE ONLY SEEMS TO STAND STILL.
teach.b: First, the tree that seems to stand still. Over a week a tree is busy: a bud swells, a leaf turns, a branch holds a bird on Monday and is empty on Tuesday, the light hits it from a new angle as the season tips.
You won't see it in one glance. You'll see it by coming back. Second, trees in the old texts.
The very first psalm has a tree in it.

teach.h: PSALM 1: A TREE BY THE WATER.
teach.b: The person who delights in the law, the psalm says, "shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season."
In his season: not a tree that fruits all year, but one that keeps its own time, and stays rooted while it waits. Third, the tree as a place to sit.
Buddhist tradition tells of Siddhartha sitting beneath a tree, resolved not to get up until he understood, and awakening there.
That tree became known as the bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. In the story, the tree doesn't teach him anything. It simply holds still while he does.
Fourth, why one tree and not many. A walk in the woods is wonderful, but it's a sampler.
By day three you know where the bark is torn. By day five you notice the same branch catches the evening light.
Something ordinary becomes someone you visit, and that shift, from scenery to a companion, is a small doorway into awe.

how: Some people keep a practice of returning to the same tree or spot outdoors over days or seasons, noticing how it changes; trees also appear as images of rootedness in the Psalms and as the place of awakening in Buddhist tradition.

games.why: today's practice is the same tree, every day: one tree becomes a relationship, not scenery.

practice: Find a tree through a window or a doorway, or step outside to one; if none is near, choose one you know well from memory.
Look at it as if you'll be asked to draw it tomorrow: the shape of the trunk, where the biggest branch leaves it, the light on the leaves or the bare twigs.
You don't need to think anything about it; just meet it, and let your breathing slow.

wordCard.voice: One tree. The same tree, visited day after day, until something you walked past becomes something you know. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakening. Buddhist tradition calls the tree Siddhartha sat beneath the bodhi tree.

carryVoice: Your line: something ordinary becomes someone you visit. The psalm's tree keeps its own time, so there's no hurry. See you tomorrow.
